CLAUDE  2026-07-20 18:45:34 UTC

That's a fun scope — a chat that spins up a playable game panel per session. The key tradeoff is **template-based generation vs. true free-form code generation**: having the AI write full game code from scratch each time (real "vibecoding") gives maximum novelty but is slow, harder to sandbox safely, and prone to broken/laggy games since LLMs are inconsistent at producing bug-free interactive JS on the first try. A **hybrid** — a small library of solid, parameterized game templates (Flappy Bird, TicTacToe, Jeopardy, Wheel of Fortune) as HTML5/canvas components, where the AI uses tool-calling (similar to the pattern already in your [chatbot.py](chatbot.py)) to pick a game and customize its theme/content/difficulty per session — gets you reliable, fast, per-user-unique results without the safety/sandboxing headaches of executing arbitrary AI-generated code in the browser.

CLAUDE  2026-07-20 18:50:42 UTC
==============================================================================
Here's the shape of it — a hybrid router sitting between a small trusted game library and a free-form codegen path:

**Client (browser)**: Chat UI and Game Panel live on the same page. The panel is a sandboxed `iframe` (`sandbox="allow-scripts"`, no `allow-same-origin`, strict CSP, no network egress) so nothing it runs can touch cookies, the parent DOM, or the network. `postMessage` is the only bridge — score updates, game-over events, etc.

**Chat Orchestrator**: Same tool-calling pattern as your existing [chatbot.py](chatbot.py), but with two tools instead of one: `launch_template_game(id, config)` and `generate_custom_game(spec)`. The LLM decides per-request which path fits.

**Template Library**: Hand-built, pre-vetted games (Flappy Bird, TicTacToe, Jeopardy, Wheel of Fortune) as static HTML/canvas bundles with a config schema each (theme, difficulty, question sets, etc.). No LLM-generated code runs here, so it skips validation entirely — this is your reliable fast path.

**Codegen Service**: For anything not in the library, a coding-capable model generates a self-contained single-file HTML/JS/CSS bundle from the user's spec. This is the "true vibecoding" path — more novelty, more risk.

**Sandbox & Validator**: Only the codegen path goes through this — a static-analysis pass (deny `fetch`/`XHR`/`WebSocket`/`eval`-of-remote, size caps) and optionally a headless smoke-test render before anything reaches the user, with a fallback to a template game if generation fails or times out.

**Session Store**: Keyed by `session_id`, holds chat history + active game config/code + expiry. Redis or SQLite is plenty for an MVP.

Main tradeoff worth flagging: the codegen path is where all the real engineering risk lives (sandboxing, validation, latency, flaky output) — the template path is comparatively trivial. I'd build the template library and orchestrator first end-to-end, then bolt on codegen as an opt-in fallback rather than building both simultaneously. Want me to start scaffolding the backend (FastAPI + tool-calling + session store) or the game panel/sandbox first?

I'm settling on the tech stack: Python with FastAPI for the backend, React using Vite on the frontend, and Groq as the LLM provider with its OpenAI-compatible SDK for function calling. For the initial release, I'll include seven games in the template library—Tic-Tac-Toe, Wheel of Fortune, Flappy Bird, Card Memory Game, Matching Game, Crossword, and Kahoot.

For the implementation approach, I'm going with a code generation path that builds the full free-form game generation plus a sandbox validator, and I'll need to set up Python 3.12 and Node LTS via winget. Now I'm mapping out the folder structure—I'll create a separate `game-chat-app/` directory to keep this feature isolated from the existing unrelated files like the movie recommender, then organize the backend with routers for chat and games endpoints, an orchestrator to handle the Groq tool-calling loop, and tool definitions with a dispatcher.

For persistence and game management, I'm adding a SQLite-backed session store to track conversation history and active games per session, plus a games registry that maps game IDs to their config schemas and template paths. The library will hold individual HTML game files like tic-tac-toe, wheel of fortune, flappy bird, memory matching (card flipping), matching games (drag-based or word-definition pairing—keeping these separate since the user requested them distinctly), crossword, and rapid quiz. The codegen module will call Groq to generate self-contained HTML bundles and validate them with static analysis using a denylist regex and size cap, while Pydantic models define the request/response schemas.

On the frontend, I'm building a Vite React app with a chat window component, message list, input field, and a game panel that hosts games in a sandboxed iframe with postMessage communication. The API client wraps fetch calls to the backend endpoints, and I'm keeping each template game genuinely simple—single self-contained HTML files with inline JS and CSS, no external dependencies. Games will be parameterized via a small JSON config injected server-side, either through a query string, a window global variable, or fetched from an endpoint.

For serving, I'm designing a single backend endpoint that returns the active game's full HTML bundle with injected configuration. For template games, the backend reads the static HTML file, injects a script tag with the config before the closing head tag, and returns the complete HTML string. Generated games return their stored HTML directly. The frontend then uses `iframe.srcdoc` to load the HTML, keeping everything uniformly sandboxed without needing separate cross-origin serving routes.

For persistence, I'm using SQLite with a minimal schema—just a single `sessions` table storing the session ID, chat history as a JSON blob, the active game bundle as a JSON blob, and an updated timestamp. This keeps the prototype lightweight without extra dependencies.

Now I'm setting up the tool-calling orchestrator that mirrors the chatbot logic with a TOOLS list...

The two main tools are `launch_template_game` for predefined games like tic-tac-toe, wheel of fortune, flappy bird, memory match, matching game, crossword, and rapid quiz, and `generate_custom_game` for novel requests. The system prompt guides the model to prefer templates but fall back to custom generation when needed. When launching a template, I validate the game ID against the registry, merge the config with defaults, store it as the active game in the session, and signal back that the game is ready. For custom games, I call the code generator which prompts a stronger model to produce a single HTML file.

The validator then checks that HTML against a size limit and blocks dangerous patterns like fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, import, eval, document.cookie, and window access. If validation fails, I retry once with feedback; if it fails again, I return a fallback message suggesting the template games instead. On success, the game gets stored as active.

The API has a POST endpoint for chat that runs the orchestrator loop and returns the reply plus game readiness info, and a GET endpoint that returns the current game bundle with the HTML assembled and config injected. Sessions are created client-side as UUIDs stored in localStorage and sent with every request.

On the frontend, I retrieve or create the session ID on load, then the chat window sends messages to the POST endpoint. When the response indicates the game is ready, the game panel fetches the bundle and loads the HTML into an iframe. The iframe posts messages back about score and game-over events; I'll listen for those and display a minimal score HUD since that's a core part of the deliverable. For the iframe itself, I'm setting up sandboxing with `allow-scripts` only, blocking same-origin access and navigation, then injecting a strict Content Security Policy meta tag server-side that allows only inline scripts and styles while blocking all network requests—this ensures the game can't exfiltrate data or make external calls.

On top of that, I'm running a denylist validator against the generated code to catch dangerous patterns like `eval`, `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, and any external script or stylesheet references, plus enforcing a size cap and requiring everything to be self-contained. With seven template games, codegen, and the React frontend all in play, I need these layered defenses to keep things tight.

Given the scope here—backend, sandboxing, Groq integration, Python/Node setup—I'll structure this as an iterative build: core backend first, then one game to validate the pipeline, then the rest of the games, codegen, and frontend. I'll keep each game genuinely minimal and self-contained, matching the "simple games" requirement, and use task tracking to manage all the moving pieces as I go.

For the game types, I'm settling on memory_match as the card-flip pairs game to keep the naming clear.

For the remaining games: matching_game pairs items from two columns (term ↔ definition style), crossword is a simple grid with word list and clues to validate, rapid_quiz is timed multiple-choice with score and streak tracking (no multiplayer needed for single-user), and wheel_of_fortune is letter/word guessing with a limited guess count.

Flappy bird uses canvas with gravity physics, pipe spawning, and collision detection via bounding boxes. Tic-tac-toe is a 3x3 grid against a configurable AI opponent (minimax for hard difficulty, random for easy). Each game accepts a config schema with game-specific settings like difficulty level, player symbol, theme, and phrase data.

The Groq LLM generates the actual game content—trivia questions, crossword clues, wheel-of-fortune phrases—based on what the user requests in chat.

All work is complete and verified live in the browser. Summary of what changed:

**Restructured UX**: Library is now the default view — a grid of 8 cards (7 templates + any AI-generated games from this session). The codegen prompt tells the model to build on the same tokens, and the outer app chrome uses the identical palette.

**Bug found and fixed along the way**: the first live codegen test produced a game with `var(--accent)` used as a bare JS expression (invalid — that's CSS-only syntax), which silently crashed the whole game with a blank screen. Fixed at both ends: tightened the codegen prompt to explain the CSS-vs-JS distinction, and added a real safety net — [validator.py](game-chat-app/backend/app/codegen/validator.py) now runs `node --check` on generated JavaScript before ever serving it, with the concrete syntax error fed back to the model for an automatic retry. This stays mechanically faithful to the original while layering in the educational decision-making. I'm reconsidering the design—the two-gap approach is cleaner from a genre perspective, but I realize keeping it simple with one gap per pipe and just labeling the answer choices is actually more robust and easier to implement correctly. # PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## Quick Reference

| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Merge PDFs | pypdf | `writer.add_page(page)` |
| Split PDFs | pypdf | One page per file |
| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
| Create PDFs | reportlab | Canvas or Platypus |
| Command line merge | qpdf | `qpdf --empty --pages ...` |
| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
| Fill PDF forms | pdf-lib or pypdf (see FORMS.md) | See FORMS.md |

**New backend module** ([backend/app/learning/](prototype-generator/backend/app/learning/)):
- `knowledge_base.py` — real, accurate AZ-900 content across the 3 exam domains (Cloud Concepts, Azure Architecture & Services, Azure Management & Governance): ~7 grounding facts and ~7 human-authored MCQs per domain, each question tied to a fact so misses get a real, non-hallucinated explanation.

- 4 new endpoints under `/api/az900/*`, wired into `main.py`.

**Frontend**: a new "📘 AZ-900 Prep" flow — dashboard with live mastery bars, a 5-question diagnostic, and a results modal with grounded per-question explanations — reusing the existing `PlayView`/sandboxed-iframe for the actual generated game (zero new game-rendering code).

And in-game score reporting (`/game/complete`) isn't built yet — none of the 7 games report results back to the backend, so mastery updates come from the diagnostic/re-diagnostic cycle for now.

**Verified live**: curl-level checks for scoring correctness, single-use assessment enforcement, weak-domain detection, and sampling variety — then the full browser flow: took the diagnostic (answered one wrong on purpose), got 4/5 with the correct weak domain and a real grounded explanation, launched the practice game (confirmed its content was actually grounded in Azure Architecture & Services facts), and confirmed the mastery bars updated correctly on return. For Memory Match, I need to define what "correct/total" means as a scoring metric. Since the game always has a winning state with no way to lose, efficiency matters most—fewer moves means better performance. I'm considering tracking perfect matches (pairs found on the first attempt without having seen either card before) against the total number of pairs, though that gets complicated to implement cleanly.

A simpler approach: use moves as the denominator and matched pairs as the numerator. If every move results in a match, that's 100% efficiency; if some moves are wrong guesses, the ratio drops accordingly. This gives a genuine performance signal using data I'm already tracking (moves and matchedCount), so I'll report those values to the game result handler when the game finishes.

     ```tsx
       const gameId = az900GameId;

       const reportResult = onGameResult;
       function handleMessage(event: MessageEvent) {
         if (event.source !== iframeRef.current?.contentWindow) return;
         const data = event.data;
         if (!data || data.source !== "game-engine" || data.type !== "game-result") return;

         reportResult({ gameId, domain, correct, total });
         setResultBanner(`✓ Result recorded: ${correct}/${total}`);
       }
       window.addEventListener("message", handleMessage);
       return () => window.removeEventListener("message", handleMessage);
     }, [az900GameId, az900Domain, game.gameId]);
     ```

## AZ-900: Skills Measured (official, as of July 20, 2026)

**Passing score: 700/1000.** Format: ~40-60 questions, ~60 min exam time within an ~85 min session.

### Describe cloud concepts (25–30%)
**Describe cloud computing**
- Define cloud computing
- Describe the shared responsibility model
- Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid
- Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
- Describe the consumption-based model
- Compare cloud pricing models
- Describe serverless

**Describe the benefits of using cloud services**
- Benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
- Benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud
- Benefits of security and governance in the cloud
- Benefits of manageability in the cloud

**Describe cloud service types**
- Describe IaaS
- Describe PaaS
- Describe SaaS
- Identify appropriate use cases for each (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS)

### Describe Azure architecture and services (35–40%)
**Core architectural components**
- Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
- Availability zones
- Azure datacenters
- Azure resources and resource groups
- Subscriptions
- Management groups
- Hierarchy of resource groups, subscriptions, and management groups

**Compute and networking services**
- Compare compute types: containers, VMs, functions
- VM options: Azure VMs, VM Scale Sets, availability sets, Azure Virtual Desktop
- Resources required for virtual machines
- App hosting options: web apps, containers, VMs
- Virtual networking: VNets, subnets, peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute
- Public and private endpoints

**Storage services**
- Compare Azure Storage services
- Storage tiers
- Redundancy options
- Storage account options and storage types
- Moving files: AzCopy, Azure Storage Explorer, Azure File Sync
- Migration options: Azure Migrate, Azure Data Box

**Identity, access, and security**
- Directory services: Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Entra Domain Services
- Authentication methods: SSO, MFA, passwordless
- External identities in Azure
- Microsoft Entra Conditional Access
- Azure RBAC
- Zero Trust concept
- Defense-in-depth model
- Purpose of Microsoft Defender for Cloud

### Describe Azure management and governance (30–35%)
**Cost management**
- Factors affecting Azure costs
- Pricing calculator
- Cost management capabilities
- Purpose of tags

**Governance and compliance**
- Purpose of Microsoft Purview in Azure
- Purpose of Azure Policy
- Purpose of resource locks

**Managing and deploying resources**
- Azure portal
- Azure Cloud Shell, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell
- Purpose of Azure Arc
- Infrastructure as code (IaC)
- Azure Resource Manager (ARM) and ARM templates

**Monitoring tools**
- Purpose of Azure Advisor
- Azure Service Health
- Azure Monitor, including Log Analytics, alerts, Application Insights

The correct answer is that encryption at rest protects stored data while encryption in transit protects data moving between systems. Azure Key Vault is primarily used for securely storing and controlling access to secrets, encryption keys, and certificates in a centralized location. Now I'm looking at why embedding secrets directly in application code is problematic...

Storing secrets hard-coded in application code or configuration files significantly increases the risk of exposing credentials and weakens overall secret governance compared to using a centralized service like Key Vault. Finally, I'm identifying what Azure Key Vault doesn't manage—physical datacenter cooling systems fall outside its scope, as it focuses on digital secrets, encryption keys, and certificates.

Centralized key management provides crucial security benefits by controlling who can access keys, enabling key rotation over time, and maintaining audit trails of usage for compliance purposes. Moving on to the next question about how a line-of-business application handles customer data across Azure Storage and SQL while transmitting between services.

Both data at rest and in transit need encryption to maintain a strong security posture. For Key Vault specifically, setting up key rotation policies with alerting ensures teams get notified before keys expire, preventing unexpected service disruptions.

Now I'm looking at cost optimization strategies in Azure, starting with how Reservations work for stable workloads where customers commit to specific resource capacity over one or three years in exchange for discounts. There's also the Azure savings plan for compute, which offers more flexibility by letting customers commit to an hourly spend amount rather than locking into a specific VM type, so the discount applies more broadly across eligible compute resources.

Spot Virtual Machines are another option for fault-tolerant workloads that can handle interruptions, since they use unused Azure capacity at much lower prices. The key decision pattern depends on the workload: Reservations for predictable, long-running needs; savings plans for steady usage that needs flexibility across different compute services; and Spot pricing for interruptible workloads where cost is the priority. I'm also noting that workload requirements aren't fixed—something that starts as interruptible might become business-critical and need to shift to a more stable pricing model, or a stable workload might move from on-demand to a commitment-based approach for better long-term efficiency.

Moving on to the next questions, I'm considering which pricing option works best for fault-tolerant batch rendering jobs that can handle interruptions—Spot Virtual Machines are ideal here since they're designed for interruptible workloads. I'm also thinking through why a workload might need to transition from Spot pricing to something more predictable—as a workload becomes more business-critical and less tolerant of interruptions, the cost savings of Spot pricing become less important than reliability.

**What got merged into `knowledge_base.py`:**
- All 933 authored items collapsed down to **499 unique facts (`SNIPPETS`) + 434 practice questions (`QUESTION_BANK`)** across 62 topics (the official 57 skill bullets + the 5 extra topics I found), replacing the old ~30-item hand-typed starter set entirely.

- Rewrote the file's docstring to document where the content actually came from and point to `content_bank/*.json` as the audit trail for citations.

**Wired the real weighting through the app** (none of this existed before):
- `service.py`'s diagnostic now samples questions **proportional to real exam weight** via a largest-remainder split — verified live: a 10-question diagnostic comes out 4 Architecture / 3 Cloud Concepts / 3 Management, not an even 3-3-4.
- `service.py`'s overall progress bar is now a **weighted average**, not a flat 1/3 each — verified twice in the browser with exact hand-checked math (21% and 42% at two different mastery states, both matching the formula precisely).
- `submit_assessment` now shows each wrong answer's **own specific explanation** (all 434 questions have one) instead of a generic topic-level snippet — confirmed live with real explanations like "Data Box Heavy is a ruggedized physical device built to move petabyte-scale data sets offline."
- Caught and fixed one real bug before it shipped: `orchestrator.py`'s chat system prompt was dumping *every* snippet into *every* chat turn — fine at 30 facts, would have been ~25,000 tokens of waste per message at 499. Capped it to 2 facts/topic (127 lines, ~6.5k tokens) while keeping every topic represented.

**Ran it end-to-end in the browser** (fresh session): gate → diagnostic → submit → weighted progress bar → launched a practice activity grounded in the new content → real score reported → mastery and weak-areas correctly recalculated. Zero console errors at any step. Backend and frontend are both up now at `localhost:8000` / `localhost:5173`.

Since coverage only ever grows but accuracy is a live ratio, the ceiling rises monotonically while the actual number underneath can go up or down with real performance.

A topic now needs **2 correct answers in a row** to count toward the progress bar; a single miss resets that topic's streak to 0 immediately, even if it was already mastered. - A perfect first diagnostic → **0% mastered** (nothing hits streak 2 yet).
- Two passing practice rounds on the same topics → mastery climbs (1 → 5 topics mastered, watched live).
- Isolated test: 90% mastery → a bad round → **50%**, proving real progress loss, not just diluted averaging.
- The diagnostic and practice-content generator now both prioritize not-yet-mastered topics first, so retaking either is actually the path to 100%, not a re-roll of what's already known.

       ```python
       """
       registry.py
       ------------
       Maps a game_id (what the frontend/backend pass around everywhere — Game
       Menu cards, launch requests, practice results) to its template HTML file
       and default config. Two callers depend on this file:
       
         - learning/service.py's generate_practice_content() looks up a game_id's
           template file and merges its own AZ-900-grounded config on top of
           `defaults` via merge_config() below...
         - learning/service.py's record_practice_result() reads `mastery_weight`
           to decide how strongly one game's real score should move the domain
           mastery accumulator...
       
       EACH ENTRY IN GAMES:
         title          — shown on the Game Menu card...
         file           — the HTML filename under games/library/...
         description    — shown on the Game Menu card...
         learning_mode  — a free-text label describing the pedagogical style...
         mastery_weight — how strongly this game's real score moves domain_mastery...
         defaults       — the config a template renders with if nothing else is supplied...
       """
       ```
     - Added docstrings to `list_templates()`, `load_template_html()`, and `merge_config()` — the latter explicitly explains the falsy-value-skip logic:
       ```python
       def merge_config(game_id: str, config: dict) -> dict:
           """Overlay `config` on top of this game_id's `defaults`, key by key —
           NOT a shallow dict merge that would silently keep an empty/falsy value
           from `config` and hide the default underneath it. Any key in `config`
           that's None/""/[]/{} is treated as "didn't actually supply this" and the
           default shows through instead — this is what makes a partial or failed
           LLM generation degrade gracefully to real, curated content instead of a
           game rendering half-empty..."""
           defaults = GAMES[game_id]["defaults"]
           config = config or {}
           merged = dict(defaults)
           for key, value in config.items():
               if value not in (None, "", [], {}):
                   merged[key] = value
           return merged
       ```

   - **`frontend/src/components/Az900RecommendationCard.tsx`** — READ then fully REWRITTEN via `Write` (was severely minified/unreadable, e.g. `interface Props { sessionId:string; recommendation:RecommendedActivityApi; onPlay:(game:PlayingGame,id:string,domain:string)=>void; }` all on one line, and the whole component body crammed into ~4 lines with no comments).
     - New full content:
       ```tsx
       /**
        * Az900RecommendationCard.tsx
        * -----------------------------
        * The highlighted "do this next" banner at the top of the Game Menu (see
        * Az900GameWindow.tsx) — a shortcut around the normal card-click ->
        * Az900DomainPicker flow. `recommendation` comes straight from the backend
        * (learning/service.py's _recommend_next_activity, part of every dashboard
        * response) and already carries a chosen game_id + domain, so this
        * component only needs to launch it, not ask the learner to pick anything.
        *
        * Not shown at all if there's no recommendation to make (see
        * Az900GameWindow's `{recommendation && ...}` guard) — that only happens if
        * the dashboard fetch is still loading or genuinely returned none.
        */
       
       import { useState } from "react";
       import { generatePracticeContent } from "../api/client";
       import type { RecommendedActivityApi } from "../api/client";
       import type { PlayingGame } from "../types";
       
       interface Props {
         sessionId: string;
         recommendation: RecommendedActivityApi;
         onPlay: (game: PlayingGame, gameId: string, domain: string) => void;
       }
       
       export default function Az900RecommendationCard({ sessionId, recommendation, onPlay }: Props) {
         const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
         const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
       
         /** Generate AZ-900-grounded content for the recommended game_id/domain
          * (same generatePracticeContent call every other launch path in the app
          * uses — see Az900GameMenu.tsx) and hand off to PlayView. */
         async function launch() {
           setBusy(true);
           setError(null);
           try {
             const res = await generatePracticeContent(sessionId, recommendation.gameId, recommendation.domain);
             onPlay(
               { gameId: res.game_id, gameType: res.game_type as "template" | "generated" },
               res.game_id,
               res.domain
             );
           } catch {
             setError("Could not generate the recommended activity. Please try again.");
           } finally {
             setBusy(false);
           }
         }
       
         return (
           <section className="recommendation-card">
             <div>
               <div className="game-meta">Recommended next activity</div>
               <h3>{recommendation.gameLabel}</h3>
               <p>
                 <strong>{recommendation.domain}</strong> · {recommendation.difficulty} · {recommendation.masteryPct}%
                 mastery
               </p>
               <p>{recommendation.reason}</p>
               {error && <p className="error">{error}</p>}
             </div>
             <button className="btn" disabled={busy} onClick={launch}>
               {busy ? "Preparing…" : "Start recommendation"}
             </button>
           </section>
         );
       }
       ```

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
